_readme: This file defines the channel's style for the video generation agent. All scripts, scenes, thumbnails, and metadata must align with the Applied Philosophy, Psychology, and Stoicism niche and the meditative minimalist visual tone defined here.

reference_sample.title: The Stoic Trick Your Mind Uses to Quietly Destroy Your Future
reference_sample.style_summary: Dark cinematic minimalism with single warm light sources, ancient stone and parchment textures, sparse symbolic objects, and a slow meditative pace that rewards contemplative viewers.

channel.name: Eternal Wisdom
channel.niche: Applied Philosophy, Psychology, and Stoicism — practical ancient wisdom reframed through modern psychological research
channel.target_audience: Thoughtful 28-50 year olds who feel intellectually under-stimulated, are quietly struggling with anxiety, ambition, or meaning, and who distrust motivational content but are deeply drawn to rigorous ideas that actually change how they think. Professionals, readers, and former students who want philosophy that applies on a Tuesday morning.
channel.tone: Calm, precise, slightly unsettling. Sounds like a philosopher who has genuinely thought about this for years and is finally telling you the part everyone else skips. Not motivational. Not lecturing. Intimate and unhurried, like a late-night conversation that changes something permanently.

host.name: Elias
host.personality: Elias is deeply read, unhurried, and a little austere. He does not comfort the viewer — he asks them to see something clearly. He has genuine respect for the ancient thinkers and treats Stoicism, Existentialism, and depth psychology not as self-help tools but as precision instruments for understanding the human condition. He is never angry, never urgent, never flashy. His power comes entirely from stillness and the weight of a well-placed observation.
host.narration_style: Slow, deliberate, meditative. Long sentences that build carefully, broken occasionally by a single short line that lands like a stone dropped in still water. He uses the second person 'you' to make abstract philosophy feel personally addressed. He names the philosophers and their ideas with quiet authority, never summarizing — always deepening. Pacing is 20-30% slower than typical YouTube narration. Silence and breath are part of the delivery.
signature_phrases: The Stoics understood something about this that took me years to accept
Most people never reach this question. You are reaching it now
This is where the philosophy stops being comfortable
Epictetus did not say this to inspire you. He said it to stop you
There is a word for this in the ancient texts
Sit with that for a moment
This is the part they never put on the poster
host.physical_description: A contemplative middle-aged man with sharp classical features, short dark hair with distinguished silver temples, a calm and focused gaze that suggests deep thought rather than emotion. He wears a simple dark collarless shirt or dark turtleneck. Rendered in a semi-realistic painted portrait style with soft chiaroscuro lighting — warm amber from one side, deep shadow on the other. No smile. Expression is composed, intelligent, slightly melancholic.
host.broll_note: B-roll uses no host figure. Scenes are composed of symbolic still-life objects: open ancient books, single candles, hourglasses, worn stone surfaces, empty corridors, still water, shadows of tree branches, classical sculpture fragments, aged parchment, ink spreading in water. No people, no modern environments, no bright colors. Every image should feel like it belongs in a museum of the mind.

visual_style.photographic_style: Cinematic still-life photography meets classical oil painting aesthetics — deeply shadowed compositions with a single warm amber or cool silver light source illuminating sparse symbolic objects against near-black backgrounds
visual_style.color_palette: Near-black and deep charcoal as dominant background tones. Warm amber and aged gold for primary light and accent. Cool blue-grey for secondary philosophical or introspective scenes. Faded ivory or aged parchment white for neutral elements. Absolute avoidance of saturated primary colors, bright backgrounds, or modern visual noise.
visual_style.lighting: Single directional light source only — either warm candlelight amber from below or one side, or cool diffused silver from above suggesting moonlight or dawn. Deep chiaroscuro shadows occupying 60-70% of the frame. No fill lights. No flat even lighting. Darkness is compositional, not accidental.
visual_style.camera: Centered or slightly off-center compositions with extreme negative space. Low angles for objects that convey weight and permanence. Tight detail shots of textures: the grain of stone, the edge of a page, the surface of still water. Shallow depth of field with soft bokeh on backgrounds. No dynamic movement implied — every composition feels paused, suspended, eternal.
visual_style.texture: Heavy emphasis on physical texture: worn stone, aged parchment, rough linen, cracked marble, oxidized bronze, candle wax drips, ink-stained paper. Subtle film grain overlay on all images to add temporal depth. No smooth digital surfaces, no plastic or glass, no modern materials.
visual_style.mood: Meditative, austere, timeless, slightly melancholic — the feeling of sitting alone in an ancient library at night and understanding something irreversible about yourself
scene_rules: Use near-black or deep charcoal backgrounds for all primary scenes. No white or bright backgrounds.
Every scene must contain exactly one primary symbolic object: a candle, an hourglass, a stone, an open book, a quill, a cracked column, still water, or a fragment of classical sculpture.
Use amber and warm gold for scenes about action, virtue, and agency. Use cool blue-grey for scenes about mortality, impermanence, and acceptance.
No photorealistic modern humans, no contemporary settings, no digital devices, no bright artificial light sources.
Text inside scene images is strictly forbidden. No labels, no captions, no UI elements within the generated image.
Depth of field must always leave the background in soft focus. The symbolic object in the foreground is sharp; everything else dissolves.
Alternate between extreme close-up detail shots (texture of stone, single flame, ink on parchment) and wider sparse compositions to control pacing rhythm.
Every image must feel as though it could have been painted in the 17th century — timeless, not dateable.
visual_style.style_suffix_base: Cinematic dark minimalist photography, single warm amber candlelight or cool silver moonlight as sole light source, deep charcoal and near-black backgrounds with chiaroscuro shadows occupying 60% of frame, sparse symbolic still-life composition, single ancient or natural object in sharp focus, subtle film grain, shallow depth of field, aged parchment and worn stone textures, no text, no people, no modern objects, meditative and austere mood, oil painting meets cinematic photography aesthetic, 16:9 aspect ratio.
visual_style.style_guide_note: This channel's visual language must feel like the interior of a mind that has been thinking for a very long time. Resist any impulse toward dynamism, color, or modernity. If an image could appear in a YouTube finance video or a tech explainer, it is wrong for this channel. If it could hang in a gallery of Dutch Golden Age still-life paintings, it is correct.

script_style.hook_pattern: Open with a single precise observation about human psychology or a named philosophical idea that immediately creates a sense of uncomfortable recognition. Do not announce the topic — embody it. The first sentence should make the viewer feel that they have been quietly understood by someone who has thought about this far longer than they have.
opening_examples: The Stoics had a name for the thing you did this morning — the thing you told yourself was fine.
Every major school of ancient philosophy independently arrived at the same diagnosis of the human mind. And the diagnosis is not flattering.
Marcus Aurelius wrote something in his private journal that he never intended anyone to read. And it is the most psychologically precise thing ever written about why most people never change.
There is a specific kind of suffering that has no name in modern psychology. The Stoics named it two thousand years ago. And you have been living inside it.
structure: The unsettling opening observation — a precise psychological or philosophical truth stated plainly, without preamble
Naming the ancient framework — introducing the specific Stoic, Existentialist, or philosophical concept with genuine depth, not summary
The modern psychological mirror — showing how current research in cognitive psychology or behavioral science confirms what the ancients observed
The mechanism exposed — explaining the specific internal process at work, using concrete human examples without being personal or confessional
The cost of not seeing it — articulating clearly and calmly what this misunderstanding has already taken and will continue to take
The philosophical response — not a solution, but a reorientation. What the Stoics or the philosophical tradition actually prescribes as the correct relationship with this reality
The reflective close — a single final thought that reframes the entire video and leaves the viewer sitting with something they cannot immediately resolve
retention_devices: The named-concept loop: introduce an ancient Greek or Latin term early without defining it fully, promise to return to it, complete the definition at the 70% mark as a payoff
The uncomfortable specificity: describe a human behavior or thought pattern so precisely that viewers recognize themselves without being addressed directly
The philosophical paradox bridge: pose a question at the end of a section that appears unanswerable, then transition by saying this is where it becomes interesting
The quote as structural anchor: open a section with a verbatim ancient quote, spend the next two minutes unpacking what it actually means versus what most people assume
The inversion: take a widely accepted piece of modern self-help wisdom and demonstrate, using Stoic or philosophical logic, precisely why it leads to the opposite of its intended effect
script_style.cta_style: Place a single quiet, non-urgent subscription mention at approximately the 25% mark, framed as an intellectual community rather than a channel growth appeal. Example: 'If this kind of thinking is useful to you, there is more of it here.' Never use hard-sell language, never repeat the CTA, never place it at the end over a loud outro. The monetization strategy depends on completion rate, not click-throughs — do nothing that interrupts the meditative flow.

youtube_metadata._readme: Metadata for Eternal Wisdom. Titles must provoke immediate intellectual curiosity and Browse Feature clicks from premium demographics. Descriptions function as standalone philosophical summaries. Tags target the intersection of philosophy, psychology, and self-understanding.

title_style.format: A precise psychological or philosophical observation as a declarative statement, followed by parenthetical consequence or ancient source — OR — a grand unresolved question that implies the answer will be uncomfortable
examples: The Stoic Trick Your Mind Uses to Quietly Destroy Your Future
Why Marcus Aurelius Said Most People Never Actually Think (He Was Right)
The Ancient Name for the Thing That Is Quietly Exhausting You
What Epictetus Understood About Anxiety That Modern Psychology Still Misses
The Philosophical Reason You Cannot Stop Thinking (And What To Do Instead)
Why the Stoics Believed Most People Are Asleep (Even While Awake)
rules: Never use motivational or positive framing — the title must create intellectual tension, not promise transformation
Include a named philosopher or ancient school when possible to signal depth and credibility
Keep titles under 70 characters for full display in search and Browse
Use parentheses to add a consequence, source citation, or unsettling qualifier that deepens the hook
Avoid questions that can be answered with yes or no — use questions that imply a disturbing or counterintuitive answer

description_style.format: Two to three paragraphs. First paragraph states the central philosophical problem and names the ancient framework. Second paragraph describes the psychological mechanism explored. Third paragraph names the specific ancient thinkers referenced and ends with a value promise for the viewer.
rules: Open with the philosophical problem, not a summary of the video content
Name at least one ancient philosopher and one specific philosophical concept in the first paragraph
Never use bullet points or lists — the description should read as intellectual prose
End with a quiet value statement, not a call to action
Keep total description under 300 words to maintain density and quality signals
description_style.example:
The Stoics identified a specific failure mode of the human mind — one they considered more dangerous than passion, more corrosive than vice, and almost impossible to see from the inside. They called it the fog of the ordinary. And they believed it was the primary reason most people never become who they are capable of being.

This video examines the psychological mechanism behind what Marcus Aurelius described in Book Four of the Meditations as the mind's tendency to mistake movement for direction. Drawing on Stoic philosophy and modern research in cognitive psychology, we explore precisely how this pattern operates, why it feels indistinguishable from genuine progress, and what the ancient framework actually prescribes as the corrective — which is not what most people expect.

Referencing Marcus Aurelius, Epictetus, and the foundational principles of Stoic psychology, this is a rigorous examination of a human problem that has not changed in two thousand years.

rules: Lead with the specific philosophical school or thinker featured in the video
Include the psychological concept or mechanism explored
Add broad discoverability tags for the Philosophy and Psychology crossover audience
Never use generic self-help tags — this channel targets a premium intellectual demographic and broad tags attract mismatched audiences
